title: Faith not meritorious cause; first justification mere grace (Trent sess. 6 ch. 8)
source_text: XLIV. Praeterea Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae agnoscunt fidem non justificare, tanquam causam meritoriam remissionis peccatorum nostrorum, & doni justitiae: quumque homo ex statu peccati in statum gratiae transfertur, justificationem ejus esse mere gratuitam, nec ullis nostris meritis deberi, sed divinae gratiae, per Christi solius merita nobis partae, unice esse ascribendam. Quod expresse definivit Concilium Tridentinum, eadem Sess. 6. cap. 8. Gratis autem ideo justificari dicimur, inquit, quia nihil eorum quae justificationem praecedunt, sive fides, sive opera, ipsam justificationis gratiam promeretur; si enim gratia est, jam non ex operibus: alioquin, ut Apostolus inquit, gratia jam non est gratia.
pass_a_gloss: Further, the Doctors of the Roman Church acknowledge that faith does not justify as a meritorious cause of the remission of our sins and of the gift of righteousness: and that when a man is transferred from the state of sin into the state of grace, his justification is merely gratuitous, owed to none of our merits, but is to be ascribed uniquely to divine grace obtained for us through Christ's merits alone. Which the Council of Trent expressly defined in the same Session 6, chapter 8. But we are said to be justified freely, it says, because nothing of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification itself; for if it is grace, it is no longer from works: otherwise, as the Apostle says, grace is no longer grace.
pass_b_english: Rome: faith is not the meritorious cause; passage into grace is mere gift through Christ alone.
Trent: nothing preceding justification—faith or works—merits justifying grace.
